chunks.text: Japan has an overall safety risk rated as very-low. Violent crime is very-low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is low. The US State Department advises: Exercise Normal Precautions. Exercise normal precautions in Japan. U.S. citizens should always exercise caution when traveling abroad. For solo female travelers: Very safe. Some train cars have women-only sections during rush hour. Groping (chikan) on crowded trains is a known issue — women-only cars are the safest option.. LGBTQ+ safety: Generally safe but limited legal protections. Same-sex marriage not recognized. PDA is uncommon for all couples. Discrimination is rare but LGBTQ+ visibility is limited outside Tokyo's Shinjuku Ni-chome.. Natural disaster risks include: earthquakes, typhoons, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions.

In Japan, call 110 for police, 119 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 119 for fire services. Police and fire/ambulance use different numbers. English support is limited — ask hotel staff for help if possible. The U.S. Embassy Tokyo in Tokyo can be reached at +81-3-3224-5000.

Japan has a Universal (National Health Insurance) healthcare system, rated excellent quality. Typical costs for tourists: Tourists pay full price without insurance. A basic clinic visit costs $50-150. Emergency room visits $200-800. Hospital stays $300-1,000/night. Dental visits $50-200.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies (yakkyoku) are widespread. Many OTC medications available including pain relievers and cold medicine. Prescription drugs require a local prescription — foreign prescriptions are not accepted.. Hospital quality is excellent. Most staff speak limited English — major hospitals in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto have international departments with English-speaking staff. St. Luke's International Hospital (Tokyo) and AMDA International Medical Information Center can help locate English-speaking doctors. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Japanese Encephalitis (if rural/extended stay). Malaria risk is negligible. Travel insurance advice: Travel insurance strongly recommended. Japanese hospitals typically require upfront payment in cash or credit card — insurance reimbursement happens after. Medevac coverage recommended for remote areas.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Japan. Strictly prohibited under the Stimulants Control Act. Carrying even with a valid foreign prescription can result in arrest and imprisonment. There is no exemption process.
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is banned in Japan. Prohibited as it contains stimulant precursors. Use alternative decongestants like phenylephrine.
Codeine is restricted in Japan. Allowed in small quantities (up to 1 month supply) with a Yakkan Shoumei import certificate and doctor's letter.
CBD / cannabis products is banned in Japan. All cannabis-derived products are illegal regardless of THC content. CBD oil, edibles, and topicals are prohibited.
Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is restricted in Japan. Allowed with a Yakkan Shoumei import certificate. Must carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Maximum 1 month supply.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Japan. Some benzodiazepines are controlled. Allowed with Yakkan Shoumei for up to 1 month supply with documentation.

Thailand has an overall safety risk rated as low. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is moderate. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased caution in Thailand due to risk of unrest. Some areas have increased risk. Violent crime is rare against tourists but does occur. For solo female travelers: Generally safe. Exercise normal caution at night, especially on islands and in nightlife areas. Drink spiking occurs — watch your drinks. Full moon parties on Koh Phangan require extra vigilance.. LGBTQ+ safety: Very tolerant culturally. Thailand is one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries in Asia. Same-sex marriage legalized in 2024. Bangkok has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Kathoey (transgender women) are culturally visible.. Natural disaster risks include: flooding (monsoon season), tsunamis (Andaman coast), earthquakes (northern region).

In Thailand, call 191 for police, 1669 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 199 for fire services. Tourist police: 1155 (English-speaking, available 24/7). This should be your first call for non-emergency issues. The U.S. Embassy Bangkok in Bangkok can be reached at +66-2-205-4000.

Thailand has a Mixed public/private healthcare system, rated good quality. Typical costs for tourists: Private hospitals cater to medical tourists and are excellent quality. Clinic visit $30-80. Emergency room $100-500. Private hospital stay $150-500/night. Bumrungrad International Hospital (Bangkok) is world-class. Public hospitals are cheaper ($10-50) but crowded with long waits and limited English.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies are everywhere and many medications available OTC that require prescriptions in Western countries — including some antibiotics and pain medications. Pharmacists often speak basic English.. Bangkok has world-class private hospitals (Bumrungrad, Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej) popular with medical tourists. Outside Bangkok, quality drops significantly. Chiang Mai has adequate private hospitals. Islands and rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Bangkok. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (if rural), Rabies (if rural/animal contact). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: Travel insurance essential. Private hospitals require proof of insurance or cash deposit upfront ($500-2,000). Medevac coverage strongly recommended if visiting islands or rural areas.
Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Thailand. Strictly illegal. Thailand has severe drug penalties including long prison sentences. No exemption for foreign prescriptions.
CBD / cannabis products is restricted in Thailand. Cannabis was re-criminalized in 2025. CBD products with >0.2% THC are illegal. Enforcement is increasing. Do not bring any cannabis products.
Codeine is restricted in Thailand. Controlled substance. Bring prescription documentation and keep in original packaging. Maximum 30 days supply.
Tramadol is restricted in Thailand. Classified as a narcotic. Bring doctor's letter and original prescription. Keep in original packaging.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Thailand. Psychotropic substances requiring documentation. Carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Max 30-day supply.
